title: Xiaomi's Three Chips: Trading Resources for Time, Betting on a Paradigm Shift in On-Device AI
dek: Xiaomi unveiled three Xuanjie chips in one go, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking, and an all-AI architecture. It's trading resources for time, betting on a paradigm shift in on-device AI and vertical integration—but it still lags top-tier chip companies.
why: This episode offers a deep dive into the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips. It's dense with information, using clear analogies for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking. Worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors tracking Xiaomi.
who: Investors focused on Xiaomi's chip efforts, chip industry engineers, product managers, and tech professionals wanting to understand on-device AI trends.
skip: The first 3 minutes discussing the definition of self-developed chips can be skipped; jump straight to the technical analysis.

points.h: Chip capability is about system definition, not IP self-reliance
points.body: To judge whether a company can really make chips, don't just count how many IP blocks it handcrafted; look at how much system definition power it holds. Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, but system integration and physical implementation are its own. Apple and Qualcomm excel because they iterate yearly and tape out continuously—something latecomers lack. Xiaomi doesn't have a decade to learn slowly, so it's taking an aggressive path, advancing multiple high-risk technology lines simultaneously.

points.h: O1's poor energy efficiency stems from a missing shared water tank
points.body: The Xuanjie O1 lacks a system-level cache (SLC), causing power consumption to spike under heavy GPU load and hurting energy efficiency. An SLC is like a shared water tank in a residential complex: the closer data is to compute units, the faster the access and the lower the power. The O1 has many GPU cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores sit idle waiting for data—this is the bandwidth wall. The O3 adds a 16MB SLC, split into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, plus an on-chip network scheduler to handle data consistency and access conflicts.

points.h: ARM's generic bus forced Xuanjie to build its own
points.body: ARM's off-the-shelf CHI+CMN solution is too generic, retaining compatibility and redundancy that hinder customization for Xuanjie. The O3 instead uses a self-developed X-Ring unified bus that is CHI-compatible but defines its own interconnect protocol, along with a custom high-speed network hub and memory controller. This reduces protocol conversion overhead and lets data decide cache placement and paths based on needs. Xiaomi claims protocol conversion overhead drops 75%, and static access latency is 82 nanoseconds—32% lower than the O1 and even below Apple's A19 Pro.

points.h: Compute bottleneck shifts from matrix multiplication to vector operations
points.body: The O3 adds AI units to every subsystem—CPU, GPU, ISP, etc.—so computation happens where data resides, reducing data movement. NPU cores drop from 6 to 4, but tensor compute rises to 200 TOPS because Xiaomi believes the bottleneck for large models is expanding from matrix multiplication to vector operations like Softmax, quantization, and KV cache. The vector unit area is comparable to the tensor unit, with 6.8 times more multiply-accumulate units than the O1, and it introduces an SMT-like architecture similar to CUDA to handle irregular parallel tasks.

points.h: Chips and models should be co-defined by the same company
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with MEMO to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits using a 5-value quantization method, with almost no accuracy loss, cutting memory bandwidth and capacity needs by 30%. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model runs on the O3, with prefill performance up 40% and decode up 45%. This ability to co-define chips and models is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration—no waiting for others to define models before adapting.

points.h: 3nm performance is squeezed out cell by cell
points.body: The O3 uses the more mature N3P process, delivering 5% higher performance at the same power and 5%-10% lower power at the same frequency. Xiaomi also made extensive process optimizations: self-developed standard cells grew from 480 in the O1 to over 2,400, covering various chip components; power delivery buffers were compressed and routed through the middle of modules, boosting transistor density by 5%. The CPU shifted from a 4-cluster to a 3-cluster 10-core all-big-core design, improving single-core performance by 31% and multi-core by 60%, surpassing the A19 Pro.

points.h: Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
points.body: The Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking: one compute wafer plus two memory wafers stacked vertically, interconnected via hybrid bonding, forming a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical connections to achieve high bandwidth with lower energy per bit shift—like HBM for phones. Data: 28,762 data connections, 1.22TB/s bandwidth, far exceeding the tens of bits wide connections in traditional SoC-LPDDR setups. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each paired with a RISC-V processor for control.

points.h: CXMT's value lies in co-definition, not speed grades
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with CXMT to debut LPDDR6, reducing reliance on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if CXMT offers the entry-level 10.667Gbps speed grade, Xiaomi can compensate for peak rate gaps with wider channels, larger SLC, and a custom memory controller. More importantly, the two companies co-validate and tune from the design stage, jointly defining a Chinese mobile memory subsystem solution. For CXMT, this proves its high-speed I/O and PHY capabilities, earning a seat at the next-generation mobile memory table.

points.h: Xiaomi is betting not on chips but on a time window
points.body: First, it bets on a paradigm shift in on-device computing: AI's weight in SoCs is rising, phones become AI interaction gateways, and Xiaomi wants to be in the definer's seat. Second, it bets that vertical integration becomes a core competency for device makers—generic chips can't meet the fragmented needs of human, car, and home scenarios, so Xiaomi must own its compute architecture. Third, it bets on an uncertain time window, trading resources for time to compress the catch-up cycle, preferring to bear engineering risk rather than wait for the window to close.

points.h: Xuanjie is closing faster, but still hasn't cleared any of three hurdles
points.body: Top-tier SoC companies need three capabilities: self-developed CPU/GPU microarchitecture, self-developed 5G baseband, and continuous multi-generation tape-outs with tens of millions of shipments. Xuanjie currently meets none, still clearly behind the first tier—it's just catching up faster. What truly reshapes the industry isn't a single dazzling chip but the sustained iteration capability built by a group of companies. Xuanjie's larger significance is proving Xiaomi's chip efforts haven't stalled and that it's moving forward with Chinese chip industry partners.

terms.def: A cache shared by multiple compute units within a chip, like a shared water tank in a residential complex.
A wafer-level 3D stacking interconnect technology that uses direct copper connections for high bandwidth and low power.
Placing memory and compute units close together to reduce data movement distance, improving bandwidth and energy efficiency.
A performance bottleneck where data movement capability becomes the limiting factor, preventing additional compute cores from being utilized.
A parallel processing architecture that can manage multiple task groups simultaneously, improving compute unit utilization.
